messages.subject_clean: strand information for get Association and Transcript ID
messages.body_plain:
Dear Group,

I am trying to create a file where I have a Transcript ID  and the distance from the nearest strand-specific  TSS combined with each line of my  methDiff object.

I previously asked if the “getAssociationWithTSS” function gave strand-specific annotation and the answer was if I selected TRUE for “annotate.WithGenicParts” that it should.

I am finding that CG strand positon in my methDiff file does not equal the stand of the transcript ID.

myDiff is my methDiff object

gene500.obj is my GRanges list object, originally downloaded from UCSC Ensembl transcript bed file

Here is what I have done:

b1=annotate.WithGenicParts(myDiff1,gene500.obj,strand=TRUE)

e1=getAssociationWithTSS(b1)

f<-cbind(getData(myDiff1)[e1$target.row,], e1)

> head(f)

   chr start   end strand    pvalue qvalue  meth.diff target.row

1 chr1 10493 10493      + 1.0000000      1   0.000000          1

2 chr1 10497 10497      + 1.0000000      1   0.000000          2

3 chr1 10498 10498      - 0.2720307      1 -20.000000          3

4 chr1 10525 10525      + 1.0000000      1  -5.555556          4

5 chr1 10526 10526      - 0.5276653      1  -8.000000          5

6 chr1 10542 10542      + 1.0000000      1   0.000000          6

  dist.to.feature    feature.name <http://feature.name> feature.strand

1           -1376 ENST00000456328              +

2           -1372 ENST00000456328              +

3           -1371 ENST00000456328              +

4           -1344 ENST00000456328              +

5           -1343 ENST00000456328              +

6           -1327 ENST00000456328              +

What you can see is that the feature.name <http://feature.name> is the same no matter the strand of the CG, so that rows 3 and 5 are annotated incorrectly as the Transcript is on the “+” strand.

Can someone advise on what I have done incorrectly? So that I can achieve the aim of getting a myDiff file with the strand-specific closest TSS ID and distance?

Thanks,

Michelle

messages.body_plain:
sorry for the confusion, I double checked the code getAssociationWithTSS doesn't use the strand information, strand information is used when assigning DMCs/DMRs to promoters during annotate.WithGenicParts() . But also see Kalyan's reply, most of the time CpG methylation is symmetric, I don't know how much sense does it make to assign TSS using strand specificity of CpG methylation. You can easily check this by plotting the methylation difference between Cs that are covering the same CpG on opposite strands.

But here is how you can do it (you may have to do some debugging):

gene500.objP=gene500.obj
gene500.objN=gene500.obj

gene500.objP$TSSes = gene500.objP$TSSes [strand(gene500.objP$TSSes ) == "+",] # TSSes on plus strand only
gene500.objM$TSSes = gene500.objM$TSSes [strand(gene500.objM$TSSes ) == "-",] # TSSes on minus strand only

b1plus=annotate.WithGenicParts(myDiff1[myDiff1$strand=="+",],gene500.objP,strand=TRUE)

e1plus=getAssociationWithTSS(b1plus)

fplus<-cbind(getData(myDiff1)[e1plus$target.row,], e1plus)

# do a similar operation for - strand myDiff elements and gene500.objM

b1minus=annotate.WithGenicParts(myDiff1[myDiff1$strand=="-",],gene500.objP,strand=TRUE)

e1minus=getAssociationWithTSS(b1minus)

fminus<-cbind(getData(myDiff1[myDiff1$strand=="-",])[e1minus$target.row,], e1minus)

messages.subject_clean: "not enough alignments that pass coverage and phred score thresholds to calculate conversion rates"
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I keep getting this frustrating error message stating that "not enough alignments pass coverage and phred score thresholds to calculate conversion rates".

> myMethylRawList_before_normalization = read.bismark(location=bismark.files,
+                 sample.id <http://sample.id>=sample.ids,assembly=genome,
+                 save.folder=output.directory,save.context=NULL,read.context=context,
+                 nolap=FALSE,mincov=min.cov,minqual=min.qual,treatment=treatment.vector)
calling for metylation percentage per base for sample: JOH_13

not enough alignments that pass coverage and phred score thresholds to calculate conversion rates
 EXITING….

I've set the minimum coverage to O and the minqual to 0, yet I still get the same error message.

Here are the first few lines from the BAM file.

HWI-ST913:248:C4DCCACXX:5:1116:13060:95486_1:N:0:ACTTGA 99 chr1 3000723 255 50M = 3000903 216 GGGT
GTTTTTGGTTTGTTTGTTTTTTTTGTTTGTTTGTTTGTTTTTTTTG BBB<FFFFFFFFFFIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIFIIIFIIIFIIIIIIFFFFFF PG:Z:MarkDuplicatesXG:Z:CT NM:i:2 XM:Z:...z...........................................x.. XR:Z:CT XX:Z:3C43C2
HWI-ST913:248:C4DCCACXX:5:1305:13445:84678_1:N:0:ACTTGA 99 chr1 3000736 255 50M = 3000908 222 TTGT
TTGTTTTTTTTGTTTGTTTGTTTGTTTTTTTTGTTTTTTTTTTAGT BBBFFFFFFFFFFIIIFIIIIFIIFIIIFFIIIIIIFFFFFFFFFFFF7B PG:Z:MarkDuplicatesXG:Z:CT NM:i:4 XM:Z:..................................x.....hh....x... XR:Z:CT XX:Z:34C5CC4C3

I've also put in attachment an IGV screenshot showing that there is coverage.

What is the problem?
Do I have to give up on methylKit, and try another software that can handle low coverage?
Or is there a problem with the format of my BAM files?

The library preparation protocol was Agilent SureSelectXT Human Methyl-Seq
This sample has 34836504 reads aligned with Bismark with an alignment percentage of 84.0%.
I sorted the BAM files by coordinates with samtools, removed the duplicates with Picard tools' MarkDuplicates, converted the BAM files to SAM files without the header, and then sorted the SAM files.

Alexis

messages.subject_clean: "not enough alignments that pass coverage and phred score thresholds to calculate conversion rates"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alexis,

I had a similar issue in the past. For some reason, Picard mark duplicates is not compatible with the read.bismark function of MethyKit. When I changed from using Picard mark duplicates to the deduplication perl script in bismark, the SAM files were accepted by MethylKit.

You may also want to check what your depth of coverage using a separate program like picard CalculateHSMetrics to see what is your depth of coverage.

Hope this helps.

messages.subject_clean: Warning message from regional analysis with questionable results
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am following up on a previous post regarding a warning message after I had performed regional analysis. The workflow I used was:

targets= regionCounts(obj.filtered.norm , bed)
obj.meth_targets = unite(targets)
obj.mydiff_targets = calculateDiffMeth(obj.meth_targets)
obj.mydiff_targets_20p = get.methylDiff(obj.mydiff_targets, difference = 20, qvalue = 0.05)
This resulted in a warning message:

Warning message:
glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
My output was questionable as majority of the regions analysed had a p and q value of 0 when no differentially methylated cytosines was associated with the region. As such, I was wondering from this workflow (1) How are the regions calculated to be differentially methylated ?, (2) what might be the cause of the erroneous output? and (3) how I might be able to resolve this issue to get a reliable output from this analysis?

Any comments and advice would be greatly appreciated.

messages.body_plain:
I need to see the coverage values from regional methylation test, e.g row of the methylBase object that produces the warning . The file you attached doesn't help much. Just get the portion of the methylBase object that produces the warning and save it with saveRDS()

There are a couple of things that are important to consider. When you are doing tiling or regional methylation values on methylRawList then use unite(), you are potentially getting bases that don't have coverage in each sample in your tiles, so if you do the basepair resolution methylation tests then overlap those DMCs with your region of interest you may not get the same picture. Your DMRs have probably information coming from CpGs that are not covered in all samples. If you assume, methylation values don't change drastically when they are close to each other tiling or regional methylation calculation is acceptable.

Best,
Altuna

make a 3 column matrix, number of rows equal to your number of DMRs (see ?matrix). initialize with 0 or FALSE, and use %over% in GenomicRanges to create a logical vector

mat[ DMR %over% CpGi,1]=1
mat[ DMR %over% shores,2]=1
mat[ DMR %over% shelves,3]=1
colnames(mat)=c("CpGi","shores","shelves")

mat is your initialized matrix, DMR, CpGi, shores and shelves are GRanges objects. You can coerce methylKit objects to GRanges, see vignette.

Best,
Altuna

I actually lost months trying to identify the bug.

I ran bismark_deduplicate instead of Picard tools' MarkDuplicates on the SAM file outputted by Bismark, and I can now read the SAM files with methylKit.

I only have ~15% of the reads left after reduplication, so I'm actually wondering if removing the duplicates was a good idea in the first place.
I'm also wondering if more filtering would be recommended. For example, should reads where only one member of the pair align be removed?
But, these questions are not related to the problem I was having.
I'm very happy that the issue I was having has been identified and resolved.

P.S. Sorry that in reporting the issue I wrote BAM instead of SAM.

messages.subject: MethylKit PCA Analysis
messages.subject_clean: MethylKit PCA Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am using methylKit to do a methylation analysis on a MethylCAP-Bisulfite-treated sequencing data (that is, DNA fragments were pulled down with MethylCap and then, underwent bisulfite treatment followed by sequencing). I have a few questions about methylKit:

1) How does methylKit calculate PCA? Is it based on the methylation level at each base pair or does methylKit create clusters and calculates a cumulative methylation
score for a particular region or cluster and then use the methylation score for each region to do a PCA analysis? What is the information that the methylKit input to prcomp() function?

2) How can I download/capture this information (the methylation profile for each tissue sample) that methylKit submits to the prcomp() function?

3) Also, if I have certain regions of interest (for example, promoters or CpG islands) and I have their chromosomal positions in the genome, how can I get the methylation scores for these regions of interest? Using methylKit, is there a way to filter out everything so that I only have the methylation scores for these regions of interest?

4) I was told that I could get the loading matrix for the PCA from pca$rotation (see below), but there are only columns named PCA1, 2, 3, 4.......I am guessing that each number in these columns represent the "loading" (weight) for each variable for a principal component. So, shouldn't there also be a column for the variable, in this case, the variable would be the methylated regions / positions in the genome that contribute to, for example, PCA1? For example, in the PCA1 column below,  I do not know what methylated region / position has the loading of "-0.0257456039"?

Loading matrix:
PCA1
PCA2 PCA3 PCA4
-0.0257456039
-0.045478216 -0.00483179 0.0210543866
-0.0442088488
-0.0081143345 -0.0009079279 0.0350200662
-0.02690392
-0.0285829765 -0.0242796867 0.0123196758
-0.0256274555
-0.0559394237 0.0523019875 0.041726609
-0.003918779
0.0343353494 0.054446566 -0.0098142739

Thank you.

Best regards,
Jing Xian

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to repeat your question! Let me know if I got it right or not!
You have
 GRanges object 'd'
methylBase object (meth2)
You want to extract the ranges from meth2 that are either common or overlap 'd' or vice versa

In such a case I would do the following:

#Convert meth2 to GRanges

meth_ranges=as(meth2,"GRanges")

# Find intersection (in case common ranges are needed)

common=intersect(meth_ranges,d)

# Find overlaps (in case of overlaps that includes subset of ranges). Makes sure if you want to identify overlapping ranges from meth_ranges or d. One of the following will suit

overlaps_in meth_ranges=subsetByOverlaps(meth_ranges,d)

overlaps_in_d=subsetByOverlaps(d,meth_ranges)

Let us know if you got the answer!

Examples on related functions is available here <http://al2na.github.io/compgenr/genomic_intervals/granges.html>

I've had to solve a similar problem- see below for my solution modified for your situation. I think (hope?) there's a more efficient way, but this will get the job done. The basic idea is that we create a list and query by pasting all the position info together, and check for inclusion with the %in% operator.

getSites<-function(query.df, meth.base){
      dat=getData(meth.base)[ , c('chr', 'start','strand')]
      base.pos=paste(dat$chr, dat$start, dat$strand , sep='.' )

      query.pos=paste(query.df$chr, query.df$start, query.df$strand , sep='.' )

      return_indices=(1:(dim(dat)[[1]]))[ base.pos %in% query.pos ]
      output=select(meth.base, return_indices)

 }

You have to later infer the context of the Cs, using other means such as looking it up from BSgenome packages, or reading the context files as GRanges objects and using %over%

Best,

Altuna

>

As such, I get the impression that the analysis is centered on 1 of the CpG or non-CpG context at a time. Dear Altuna,
Thanks for your reply.

1) I was looking through the methylation profile file for one of my samples and I noticed that, in general, only bases that have been methylated are recorded for "coverage", "numCs", and "numTs". That is to say, that if a base was not methylated then there is generally no information about it. However, I found that on some occasions, it was reported. That is to say, I found, for example,

"chr1" 28739459  28739459 "-"  27 0 27

So, this is an unmethylated base that was reported. Why? Why does MethylKit sometimes report these unmethylated bases and sometimes throws them out. Please note that this is the methylation profile for only one sample.

2) I also noticed in https://code.google.com/p/methylkit/ that it says:
"# merge all samples to one table by using base-pair locations that are covered in all samples
# setting destrand=TRUE, will merge reads on both strans of a CpG dinucleotide. This provides better
# coverage, but only advised when looking at CpG methylation"
meth=unite(myobj,destrand=TRUE)
It says that it will use "base-pair locations that are covered in ALL samples". Therefore, am I right to understand that if I have 10 samples and for a particular location/base, 8 samples have values for "coverage", "numCs", and "numTs" but the remaining 2 samples do not have any information for this particular base, then MethylKit will not include the information for this base in the meth=unite(myobj,destrand=TRUE) function?

If this is true, isn't this criteria a little too stringent? Because of 2 samples, all information for this base would be thrown out? Can this be avoided?

3) it also says that this is "only advised when looking at CpG methylation". I am a little confused. What else can I be looking at with MethylKit if I am not looking at CpG methylation? When would I NOT use "destrand=TRUE"?

I look forward to your reply and once again, thank you for your time and patience.

Best,
Allen

Why do you think methylation is specific to only CpG dinucleotides? Where did you read that?

"DNA methylation typically occurs in a CpG <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CpG_site> dinucleotide context; non-CpG methylation is prevalent in embryonic stem cells <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stem_cell>,[5] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-5>[6] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-6>[7] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-7> and has also been indicated in neural development <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_development>."
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation

by using destrand=TRUE, you assume CpG methylation is mostly symmetric and you might gain some information on CpG dinucleotides that are covered in opposite strands in two different samples. In that case methylation levels will be on adjacent positions but opposite strands. and when using unite()  with destrand=FALSE you will lose that CpG.

I think you should read up about methylation and some basics before you start using any software relating to methylation.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I posted at the end of July a query about errors on the Ideogram graphic and got a reply about ggplot and ggplot2 command incompatibilities.

My aim is to obtain an Ideogram (both types), write it to a tiff file and save it in my space as I would for any other graphic by doing:

tiff(filename)

command(in this case the ideogram)

dev.off()

Secondly, I have been trying to faithfully follow the blog (with the changes suggested by Kalyan-- replacing "opts" with "labs") on

http://zvfak.blogspot.co.uk/2012/06/plotting-differentially-methylated.html

But I find the blog difficult to know which order I put the commands in.

I assume the following

1.       Load my diffmeth file (object called “myDiff2”)

load("4separate.myDiff.RData")

2.       Load the hg19 library

source("http://bioconductor.org/biocLite.R")

biocLite("BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg19")

library('BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg19')

3.       Define all the variables required for the ideogram

genome <-BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg19

seqlengths(genome)

chr.len = seqlengths(genome)

chr.len = chr.len[grep("_|M|X|Y", names(chr.len), invert = T)]

myIdeo <- GRanges(seqnames = names(chr.len), ranges = IRanges(start = 1,  width = chr.len))

seqlevels(myIdeo) = names(chr.len)

seqlengths(myIdeo) = (chr.len)

hypo = get.methylDiff(myDiff2, difference = 1, qvalue = 0.05, type = "hypo")

hyper = get.methylDiff(myDiff2, difference = 1, qvalue = 0.05, type = "hyper")

g.per = as(hyper, "GRanges")

seqlevels(g.per, force=TRUE) = seqlevels(myIdeo)

seqlengths(g.per)=(chr.len)

g.po = as(hypo, "GRanges")

seqlevels(g.po, force=TRUE) = seqlevels(myIdeo)

seqlengths(g.po)=(chr.len)

values(g.po)$id = "hypo"

values(g.per)$id = "hyper"

4.       Then I see I am missing the circus if/else function but am unsure how to define that in simple line-by-line script. Could I instead define two objects for cicos (“line” and “circle”) in step3 and in the function shown in step5 say circos=”line” or circus=”circle” instead of if/else?

5.       I suppose the last thing is to run the function as:

tiff('pair2.ideogram.CG.tiff', res=300, compression="lzw")

ideoDMC(myDiff2, chrom.length = chr.len, difference = 1, qvalue = 0.05, circos = FALSE, title = "test", hyper.col = "magenta", hypo.col = "green")

dev.off()

or is it:

tiff('pair2.ideogram.CG.tiff', res=300, compression="lzw")

ideoDMC <- function(myDiff2, chrom.length = chr.len, difference = 1, qvalue = 0.05, circos = FALSE, title = "test", hyper.col = "magenta", hypo.col = "green")

dev.off()

messages.body_plain:
Dear Altuna,
Thanks for your reply. I replied to you a few days ago but it seems like my post somehow never got through. Anyway, here goes again.

### How do you know most of the unmethylated bases are removed? There is no description how you achieved that control. There is coverage and quality thresholds if you are using read.bismark() function that's the only way a base would be discarded. see the doc for that function.###

I was looking at a specific gene promoter and I noticed that for a particular sample, there were no methylation data ("coverage", "numCs", "numTs") for that region. At first, I thought it may be because there were no reads for that region for this particular sample. However, when I loaded the SAM file for this sample into IGV, I noticed that there were indeed reads in this region. But I also noticed that for all the reads in this region for this sample, they were coincidentally all unmethylated (for bases where C is in the reference genome, the reads for that position were all Ts). So, I guessed that they made not have been reported because they were unmethylated. However, when I looked at methylation data for the same promoter region in another sample, I found that there were instances when the unmethylated regions were reported.

You said: "There is no description how you achieved that control."
This is only an observation. I am not sure what kind of control you are expecting.

You said: " There is coverage and quality thresholds if you are using read.bismark() function that's the only way a base would be discarded."
I used the default parameters for the read.bismark() function so I don't know if that would discard any bases. I have decided to redo this and set mincov to 10 and minqual to 0 to see if this changes anything. However, the reason I asked this question was because I thought you may know the reason for this or you may have made the same observation when you were testing your software.

###Why do you think methylation is specific to only CpG dinucleotides? Where did you read that?

"DNA methylation typically occurs in a CpG <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CpG_site> dinucleotide context; non-CpG methylation is prevalent in embryonic stem cells <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stem_cell>,[5] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-5>[6] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-6>[7] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-7> and has also been indicated in neural development <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_development>."

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation###

I think you've mis-interpreted the intent of my question. When I asked what else I could be looking at with MethylKit, I was actually thinking that perhaps your software might be able to estimate CNV. I have read that some other methylation analysis software are able to do this (see CopyNumber450K package). I could not find any mention of this in the MethylKit user guide so I decided to ask to be sure.

Best,
Allen

On Thursday, September 11, 2014 7:06:06 PM UTC+8, Altuna Akalin wrote:

> >
> > 1) I was looking through the methylation profile file for one of my samples and I noticed that, in general, only bases that have been methylated are recorded for "coverage", "numCs", and "numTs". That is to say, that if a base was not methylated then there is generally no information about it. However, I found that on some occasions, it was reported. That is to say, I found, for example,
> >
> > "chr1" 28739459  28739459 "-"  27 0 27
> >
> > So, this is an unmethylated base that was reported. Why? Why does MethylKit sometimes report these unmethylated bases and sometimes throws them out. Please note that this is the methylation profile for only one sample.
> >
>
> How do you know most of the unmethylated bases are removed? There is no description how you achieved that control. There is coverage and quality thresholds if you are using read.bismark() function that's the only way a base would be discarded. see the doc for that function.
>
>
> > 2) I also noticed in https://code.google.com/p/methylkit/ that it says:
> > "# merge all samples to one table by using base-pair locations that are covered in all samples
> > # setting destrand=TRUE, will merge reads on both strans of a CpG dinucleotide. This provides better
> > # coverage, but only advised when looking at CpG methylation"
> > meth=unite(myobj,destrand=TRUE)
> > It says that it will use "base-pair locations that are covered in ALL samples". Therefore, am I right to understand that if I have 10 samples and for a particular location/base, 8 samples have values for "coverage", "numCs", and "numTs" but the remaining 2 samples do not have any information for this particular base, then MethylKit will not include the information for this base in the meth=unite(myobj,destrand=TRUE) function?
> >
> > If this is true, isn't this criteria a little too stringent? Because of 2 samples, all information for this base would be thrown out? Can this be avoided?
>
> Please read the vignette, See page 7
>
> >
> > 3) it also says that this is "only advised when looking at CpG methylation". I am a little confused. What else can I be looking at with MethylKit if I am not looking at CpG methylation? When would I NOT use "destrand=TRUE"?
> >
> > I look forward to your reply and once again, thank you for your time and patience.
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi ,

It would seem that for the read.bismark() function, the read.context argument only allows either ’CpG’,’CHG’,’CHH’ or ’none’ to be chosen as one of the parameters. This means that the methylation events can only be investigated either in a ’CpG’,’CHG’, or ’CHH’ context. I was wondering if it is at all possible to analyse the methylation data regardless of its context, that is, to create an object that will contain ALL methylation calls whether it be in a CpG or CHG or CHH context. I was thinking that it is a little artificial to look at methylation events separately under different context. My personal feeling is that they should be looked at collectively regardless of their context.Therefore, I was wondering if there is anyway to do this in MethylKit.

Otherwise, if I generate the objects for CpG’,’CHG’, or ’CHH’ methylation data, can I then merge them into one object and use this for analysis?

Thanks,
Jingxian

messages.body_plain:
Dear Jing,

DNA methylation in CpG context is symmetric and in other contexts it is not so! In such a case, the downstream steps (like 'unite()) are not suitable to be performed on CHG and CHH contexts. In other words, even if only one strand is sequenced, methylation status on other strand could be inferred in CpG context. This is not possible in other contexts.

Also, methylation in non-CpG contexts is very minimal (almost non-existant) in a majority of cell types (except brain and stem cell related cell types).

It would also be interesting for the community to know further about your thoughts if you still have a reason to club the contexts!

Regards,
Kalyan

Dear Kalyan,
Thanks for your reply.

I understand what you are saying about DNA methylation in CpG context is symmetric and in other context like CHG or CHH it is not. I thought that when the methylation calling files goes through the unite() function, then all that happens is that the methylation calls at each position (in CpG context) for each sample is merged, for example:

"chr1" 662678 662678 "+" 46 46 0 46 34 12 17 17 0 16 16 0

Although DNA methylation on the opposite strand can be inferred, when methylKit does a PCA or Hierarchical Clustering or even when it is looking for Differentially Methylated Regions, I do not think that methylKit takes into account the methylation of C at position "662679" on the "-" strand (please correct me if I am wrong). So, although methylation on the opposite strand can be inferred, I do not think that such inferences are not used in the analysis.

If that is the case, then why not include the methylated Cs in the CHH and CHG context in the analysis? Perhaps my understanding of the analysis process is not complete but from the way I see it, there is no reason to exclude it from a global analysis of methylation.

If I am looking at embryonic stem cells where methylation has been found to occur in non-CpG context, then I personally feel that an analysis that excludes or compartmentalizes the analysis into non-CpG or CpG context to be a little "artificial".

Furthermore, this has also made me think about the destrand=TRUE argument for the unite() function. It says that "destrand=TRUE" will "merge reads on both strand of a CpG nucleotide". However, how does merging the reads on both strand of a CpG nucleotide affect the methylation call for a particular position? Say for example in position " 662678" in my example above, even if I were to merge reads from both strands, the methylation call for that position can only come from the C in the "+" strand since the same position on the opposite strand contains a G and has no methylation event.

If anyone can suggest a way to create an object that will include all methylation calls, regardless of its context, for use in the downstream analysis in methylKit please do let me know.

I look forward to your reply.

Thanks,
Jingxian

Hi,

if you are using bismark for methylation extraction, you could get the bed coverage files in three contexts separately. One can merge all the three contexts, sort the file and reformat it into methylkit input format. Then read it as if one is reading a CpG context.

Well, in the above method, methylkit would assume that we are giving it a specific context, but actually we have merged all the contexts.

hope this helps and pls be aware of the huge files and unexpected behaviour.

Regards,
Kalyan

Say for example in position " 662678" in my example above, even if I were to merge reads from both strands, the methylation call for that position can only come from the C in the "+" strand since the same position on the opposite strand contains a G and has no methylation event.
> >
> > If anyone can suggest a way to create an object that will include all methylation calls, regardless of its context, for use in the downstream analysis in methylKit please do let me know.
> >
> > I look forward to your reply.
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Jingxian
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, September 16, 2014 4:00:01 PM UTC+8, Kalyan Kumar Pasumarthy wrote:
> > > Dear Jing,
> > >
> > > DNA methylation in CpG context is symmetric and in other contexts it is not so! In such a case, the downstream steps (like 'unite()) are not suitable to be performed on CHG and CHH contexts. In other words, even if only one strand is sequenced, methylation status on other strand could be inferred in CpG context. This is not possible in other contexts.
> > >
> > > Also, methylation in non-CpG contexts is very minimal (almost non-existant) in a majority of cell types (except brain and stem cell related cell types).
> > >
> > > It would also be interesting for the community to know further about your thoughts if you still have a reason to club the contexts!
> > >
> > > Regards,
> > > Kalyan

I was thinking that it is a little artificial to look at methylation events separately under different context. My personal feeling is that they should be looked at collectively regardless of their context.Therefore, I was wondering if there is anyway to do this in MethylKit.

> I was looking at a specific gene promoter and I noticed that for a particular sample, there were no methylation data ("coverage", "numCs", "numTs") for that region. At first, I thought it may be because there were no reads for that region for this particular sample. However, when I loaded the SAM file for this sample into IGV, I noticed that there were indeed reads in this region. But I also noticed that for all the reads in this region for this sample, they were coincidentally all unmethylated (for bases where C is in the reference genome, the reads for that position were all Ts). So, I guessed that they made not have been reported because they were unmethylated. However, when I looked at methylation data for the same promoter region in another sample, I found that there were instances when the unmethylated regions were reported.
>

Yes, only thing I could think of would be coverage and quality. I can't think of anything else that would discard the reads unless there is some format issue with your sam file. For example, sorting via Picard sometimes does weird things. I would use bismark's bedgraph function see if that also gets no methylation there. If you wan't more help you need to send that portion of the sam file. If I can't replicate the problem, there is not way to fix it or even verify if there is a problem.

> You said: "There is no description how you achieved that control."
> This is only an observation. I am not sure what kind of control you are expecting.
>

Great! It is good enough, I'm just on auto-reply sometimes, similar questions asked over and over again and most of the time without explanation of how observations are done, or not even a single clue on how to replicate their problem.

> You said: " There is coverage and quality thresholds if you are using read.bismark() function that's the only way a base would be discarded."
> I used the default parameters for the read.bismark() function so I don't know if that would discard any bases. I have decided to redo this and set mincov to 10 and minqual to 0 to see if this changes anything. However, the reason I asked this question was because I thought you may know the reason for this or you may have made the same observation when you were testing your software.
>

I don't have similar observation, see the suggestions above

> ###Why do you think methylation is specific to only CpG dinucleotides? Where did you read that?
>
> "DNA methylation typically occurs in a CpG <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CpG_site> dinucleotide context; non-CpG methylation is prevalent in embryonic stem cells <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stem_cell>,[5] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-5>[6] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-6>[7] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-7> and has also been indicated in neural development <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_development>."
> http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation###
>
> I think you've mis-interpreted the intent of my question. When I asked what else I could be looking at with MethylKit, I was actually thinking that perhaps your software might be able to estimate CNV. I have read that some other methylation analysis software are able to do this (see CopyNumber450K package). I could not find any mention of this in the MethylKit user guide so I decided to ask to be sure.
>

Nope we don't, I think such a nice feature would be worth putting on the vignette if we had. To be honest, your question was open to misunderstanding :) many people asked about different methylation contexts in the past (again auto-reply habit).

 Best,
Altuna

> Best,
> Allen
>
> On Thursday, September 11, 2014 7:06:06 PM UTC+8, Altuna Akalin wrote:
> > >
> > > 1) I was looking through the methylation profile file for one of my samples and I noticed that, in general, only bases that have been methylated are recorded for "coverage", "numCs", and "numTs". That is to say, that if a base was not methylated then there is generally no information about it. However, I found that on some occasions, it was reported. That is to say, I found, for example,
> > >
> > > "chr1" 28739459  28739459 "-"  27 0 27
> > >
> > > So, this is an unmethylated base that was reported. Why? Why does MethylKit sometimes report these unmethylated bases and sometimes throws them out. Please note that this is the methylation profile for only one sample.
> > >
> >
> > How do you know most of the unmethylated bases are removed? There is no description how you achieved that control. There is coverage and quality thresholds if you are using read.bismark() function that's the only way a base would be discarded. see the doc for that function.
> >
> >
> > > 2) I also noticed in https://code.google.com/p/methylkit/ that it says:
> > > "# merge all samples to one table by using base-pair locations that are covered in all samples
> > > # setting destrand=TRUE, will merge reads on both strans of a CpG dinucleotide. This provides better
> > > # coverage, but only advised when looking at CpG methylation"
> > > meth=unite(myobj,destrand=TRUE)
> > > It says that it will use "base-pair locations that are covered in ALL samples". Therefore, am I right to understand that if I have 10 samples and for a particular location/base, 8 samples have values for "coverage", "numCs", and "numTs" but the remaining 2 samples do not have any information for this particular base, then MethylKit will not include the information for this base in the meth=unite(myobj,destrand=TRUE) function?
> > >
> > > If this is true, isn't this criteria a little too stringent? Because of 2 samples, all information for this base would be thrown out? Can this be avoided?
> >
> > Please read the vignette, See page 7
> >
> > >
> > > 3) it also says that this is "only advised when looking at CpG methylation". I am a little confused. What else can I be looking at with MethylKit if I am not looking at CpG methylation? When would I NOT use "destrand=TRUE"?
> > >
> > > I look forward to your reply and once again, thank you for your time and patience.
> >
> > Why do you think methylation is specific to only CpG dinucleotides? Where did you read that?
> >
> > "DNA methylation typically occurs in a CpG <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CpG_site> dinucleotide context; non-CpG methylation is prevalent in embryonic stem cells <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stem_cell>,[5] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-5>[6] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-6>[7] <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation#cite_note-7> and has also been indicated in neural development <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_development>."
> > http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_methylation
> >
> > by using destrand=TRUE, you assume CpG methylation is mostly symmetric and you might gain some information on CpG dinucleotides that are covered in opposite strands in two different samples. In that case methylation levels will be on adjacent positions but opposite strands. and when using unite()  with destrand=FALSE you will lose that CpG.
> >
> > I think you should read up about methylation and some basics before you start using any software relating to methylation.
> >
> > Best,
> > Altuna
> >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Thu, Sep 11, 2014 at 1:35 AM, Altuna Akalin <aak...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Therefore, my questions are:
> > > > >
> > > > > a) What is coverage1? numCs1? and numTs1? I know that they represent values for my first sample.
> > > > >
> > > > You can infer this from vignette and other sources such as presentations. If you are interested in % methylation values, use the appropriate function, it is less confusing.
> > > >
> > > > > Is "coverage" the number of times that base is covered by the sequence reads?
> > > > >
> > > > yes
> > > > > Does "numCs" represent the number of methylated cytosines (since these have not been converted by the bisulfite treatment) identified by the reads? So, for
> > > > > "chr1" 854966 854966 "+" 11 11 0 15 8 7
> > > > > In the first sample, there were 11 reads that covered this base and in all 11 reads, the base identified at this position by all 11 reads is cytosine.
> > > > >
> > > > yes
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > > Does "numTs" represent the number of thymine? As in the above example,
> > > > > "chr1" 854966 854966 "+" 11 11 0 15 8 7
> > > > >
> > > > Yes
> > > > > does this mean that of the 15 reads that covered this base at this position (854966), 7 were converted to thymine by the bisulfite treatment?
> > > > >
> > > > Yes
> > > > > b) When methylKit does a hierarchical clustering of the samples based on the methylation profile of the samples, what does it use for the to as the methylation level value? Does it use the "coverage" value or the "numCs" value or the "numTs" value or perhaps a ratio of numCs" to "numTs"? Is the hierarchical clustering based on the methylation level at EACH base pair?
> > > > >
> > > > Clustering is done using % methylation values, it uses the ratio of Cs to Cs+Ts as far as I remember
> > > >
> > > > > 2) Is it possible to produce a "heatmap" for the hierarchical clustering?
> > > > >
> > > > it wouldn't be wise to produce a heatmap for millions of methylation values. You can try it on the matrix you get from percMethylation(), i don't recommend it.
> > > >
> > > > > 3) Based on the annotation of the UCSC bed file, I noticed that
> > > > >
> > > > > "chr1" 845810 845810 "+" 12 12 0 11 11 0
> > > > > "chr1" 845816 845816 "+" 12 12 0 11 11 0
> > > > >
> > > > > belong to a single annotated CpG island. Therefore, I was wondering how can one calculate the cumulative methylation value for this CpG island?
> > > > >
> > > > Cumulative methylation values are calculated by summing up numCs and numTs for bases that overlap with that region. See examples  of such procedure at Meissner papers . You can think of that as weighted mean for the regional methylation.
> > > >
> > > > > 4) Finally, when I do the following:
> > > > >
> > > > > > getMethylationStats(myobj[[2]],plot=FALSE,both.strands=FALSE)
> > > > > methylation statistics per base
> > > > > summary:

> > > > > percentiles:

> > > > > 95% 99% 99.5% 99.9% 100%
> > > > > 100.000000 100.000000 100.000000 100.000000 100.000000
> > > > >
> > > > > At 50%, you can see the value is "5.263158". What does the value "5.263158" represent? Is this the percentage of bases that are 50% methylated? What does it mean? How do I interpret this table?
> > > > >
> > > > I suggest you read up on percentiles and quantiles for a given set of values, in this case those set of values are % methylation values per base. 50th percentile is equivalent to median. Maybe percentage signs in the output are confusing you.
> > > > http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percentile
> > > >
> > > > Best,
> > > > Altuna
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > 1) How does methylKit calculate PCA? Is it based on the methylation level at each base pair or does methylKit create clusters and calculates a cumulative methylation
> > > > > > > score for a particular region or cluster and then use the methylation score for each region to do a PCA analysis? What is the information that the methylKit input to prcomp() function?

> > > > > > with transpose=FALSE percent methylation matrix as it is goes into prcomp()

Hi Kaylan,
Actually, I just realized that I am already providing methylKit with a SAM file containing all coverage, in all 3 context. Running
bismark  [options]  <genome_folder>  {-1  <mates1>  -2  <mates2>  | <singles>}

will give a SAM file that contains  all  alignments  plus  methylation  call strings. I use this SAM file to input into MethylKit.

If one wants  to extract context-dependent (CpG/CHG/CHH) methylation, then you would need to run the bismark_methylation_extractor function which produces the 3 files you mentioned.

So the file that I input into MethylKit already contains all alignments with all Cs in all context.

The problem is that when I run read.bismark() in MethylKit, the read context require you to specify the context. And "ALL CONTEXT" is not one of the options.

That was why I am asking this question to see if I can get around this problem.

Once again, thanks for your help. I really appreciate it.

Best,
Jingxian

I thought that when the methylation calling files goes through the unite() function, then all that happens is that the methylation calls at each position (in CpG context) for each sample is merged, for example:
> > >
> > > "chr1" 662678 662678 "+" 46 46 0 46 34 12 17 17 0 16 16 0
> > >
> > > Although DNA methylation on the opposite strand can be inferred, when methylKit does a PCA or Hierarchical Clustering or even when it is looking for Differentially Methylated Regions, I do not think that methylKit takes into account the methylation of C at position "662679" on the "-" strand (please correct me if I am wrong). So, although methylation on the opposite strand can be inferred, I do not think that such inferences are not used in the analysis.
> > >
> > > If that is the case, then why not include the methylated Cs in the CHH and CHG context in the analysis? Perhaps my understanding of the analysis process is not complete but from the way I see it, there is no reason to exclude it from a global analysis of methylation.
> > >
> > > If I am looking at embryonic stem cells where methylation has been found to occur in non-CpG context, then I personally feel that an analysis that excludes or compartmentalizes the analysis into non-CpG or CpG context to be a little "artificial".
> > >
> > > Furthermore, this has also made me think about the destrand=TRUE argument for the unite() function. It says that "destrand=TRUE" will "merge reads on both strand of a CpG nucleotide". > > >

messages.body_plain:
what matters is  that the file is sorted in chromosome and read positions, but the order of chromosomes ,if it is numeric or character order, shouldn't matter. There should be blocks of sorted read positions, each block corresponding to a chromosome. Scaffolds work too, make sure that they will be interpreted as "character" by R, some string attached to numerical values works fine, such as "chr1" or "scaffold123"

Best,
ALtuna

messages.subject: Re: [methylkit_discussion] read.bismark
messages.subject_clean: [methylkit_discussion] read.bismark
messages.body_plain:
it probably won't. because, in R, we first read a couple hundred lines to decide on the column data types: numeric or character. If you don't have X and Y in those first couple hundred lines, it will think that the column is numeric. The SAM file would be OK, but the problem (I think) will arise when you try to read per base methylation information generated from the SAM file. So at that point, you can add "chr" to the appropriate columns. Or you can add it to the SAM file.

Best,
Altuna

Altuna
